t: Strong Password Checker — Greedy Case Analysis
o: We must fix three independent kinds of problems with the fewest edits: length outside [6,20], missing character categories (lower/upper/digit), and runs of 3+ identical characters. The key tension is that an insert/delete changes length while a replace fixes both a category gap and a repeating-run violation at once, so the answer is driven by which resource is scarcest. Walk through the examples: "a" has length 1 and misses two categories, so we need max(2 missing, 5 inserts) = 5 steps; "aA1" has all categories but length 3, so 3 inserts; "1337C0d3" is already strong, so 0. Since n ≤ 50, even a careful brute force over edit counts would work, but the intended solution is a linear greedy scan that classifies the password into three length regimes.
k: A single replace can simultaneously fix one missing category and shorten a bad run, so the answer is max(category gaps, run-fixing cost) once length is legal.

Runs of identical characters of length L need floor(L/3) replacements; deletions are cheaper than replacements for long runs because deleting 1, 2, or 3 characters (depending on L mod 3) removes one required replacement.
The three regimes (n < 6, 6 ≤ n ≤ 20, n > 20) have completely different optimal strategies: insert-driven, replace-driven, and delete-driven respectively.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy Simulation by Length Regime
a.i: Count missing categories m and collect runs of length ≥ 3, whose total replacement cost is R = Σ ⌊L/3⌋. If n < 6, every insert can also be chosen to fill a category, so the answer is max(m, 6−n). If 6 ≤ n ≤ 20, inserts/deletes never help, so the answer is max(m, R). If n > 20, we must delete d = n−20 characters anyway; spend them on runs first — deleting 1 char from a run with L ≡ 0 (mod 3), 2 chars from L ≡ 1, or 3 chars otherwise each removes exactly one required replacement. After spending deletions optimally, the answer is d + max(m, remaining R).
s: Compute m = number of absent categories among lowercase, uppercase, digit.
Scan the string and record the length L of every maximal run with L ≥ 3; let R = Σ L//3.
If n < 6 return max(m, 6 − n); if n ≤ 20 return max(m, R).
Otherwise set d = n − 20; iterate runs grouped by L mod 3 (0, then 1, then 2), spending min(d_remaining, chunk) deletions per run where chunk = 1, 2, 3 respectively, decrementing R by spent//3.
a.t: O(n) — one scan for categories, one for runs, and the deletion-spending loop touches each run a constant number of times.
a.sp: O(n) — the list of runs; O(1) extra beyond that.

a.i: Same regime analysis as Approach 1, but instead of three explicit passes over runs, push each run as a pair (L mod 3, L) into a min-heap. Repeatedly pop the run with the smallest residue, spend its chunk of deletions (1, 2, or 3 depending on residue), and stop when deletions run out. This makes the 'cheapest deletion first' ordering explicit and generalizes naturally if the chunk sizes were data-dependent.
s: Compute missing categories m and run lengths exactly as in Approach 1; handle n < 6 and n ≤ 20 identically.
Push (L % 3, L) for every run with L ≥ 3 into a min-heap; set d = n − 20.
While d > 0 and the heap is non-empty, pop (r, L); spend dec = min(d, r == 0 ? 1 : r == 1 ? 2 : 3) deletions, subtract dec//3 from total replacements R, decrease d by dec.
a.t: O(n log n) — building and draining the heap of runs dominates; everything else is linear.
a.sp: O(n) — the heap stores one entry per run.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1: it is optimal, linear, and shows you understand why deletes must be spent on runs with L ≡ 0 (mod 3) first. Common pitfalls: forgetting that inserts in the short-password case can double as category fixes (answer is max, not sum); treating the long-password case as pure deletion count without crediting deletions against run replacements; and mishandling runs longer than 20 (e.g., "aaaaa...a" of length 21). Edge cases to test: length 1–5 strings, all-same-character strings, strings needing both deletions and category fixes, and already-strong passwords. Likely follow-ups: what if the allowed alphabet were restricted, or if replace cost differed from insert cost — both change the greedy weighting but keep the regime structure.
